data.error.IndentationError.body: The spaces at the start of your lines (indentation) don't line up, starting from line {line}. Python uses indentation to tell which lines belong under an if or for. Check that the lines right below a line ending in a colon (:) are all indented by the same amount.
data.error.IndentationError.detective: The spaces at the start of a line look suspicious. The trail starts from line {line}. Python reads indentation to tell which lines belong to an if or for gang. Line up the lines under each colon (:) and compare: are they all indented the same?
data.error.IndentationError.title: Indentation mismatch ({type})
data.error.InputMissing.body: input() tried to read a value, but there was no input left (from line {line}). This happens when you call input() more times than the question gives inputs. Count the inputs the question gives, then count your input() calls.
data.error.InputMissing.detective: The witness has stopped talking. An input() is still waiting for an answer, and the trail starts from line {line}. Did you call input() more times than there are inputs? Compare the question's input count with your input() calls.
data.error.InputMissing.title: More input needed
data.error.NameError.body: Python doesn't recognize a name, coming from line {line}. Usually it's text that's missing its quotes: print(hello) makes Python look for a variable called hello. It can also be a typo or a variable used before it's created. If it's text, add quotes. If it's a variable, check the spelling and make sure it's set before you use it.
data.error.NameError.detective: A name with no ID has appeared! The case starts from line {line}. A string that lost its quotes (like print(hello)) may be posing as a name. Or a letter in the spelling changed, or a variable was called before it was created. Check that name's quotes, its spelling, and the line where it first shows up, one by one.
data.error.NameError.title: Unknown name ({type})
data.error.OutputLimit.body: Your code printed so much that it was stopped partway. The output came from line {line}. This happens when a print() inside a loop runs forever, or a huge number of times. Check how many times the loop runs and that it has a proper stopping condition.
data.error.OutputLimit.detective: Paper is piling up like a mountain! There was so much output that the investigation stopped. The case started with output from line {line}. Did a loop run far more times than expected, maybe forever? Track the loop count and its stopping condition.
data.error.OutputLimit.title: Too much output
data.error.SyntaxError.body: Python found something that breaks its grammar rules, coming from line {line}[[ (sometimes the real slip is on the line just before)]]. Usually a quote or bracket was opened but never closed, or the colon (:) at the end of an if or for line is missing. Check that every opening quote and bracket has a matching closing one.
data.error.SyntaxError.detective: Hmm, I see traces of broken grammar. The trail starts from line {line}[[ (the line just before it looks suspicious too)]]. The suspects: a quote that lost its partner, an unclosed bracket, a missing colon (:). Grab your magnifying glass and match each opening symbol with its closing one.
data.error.SyntaxError.title: Broken syntax ({type})
data.error.Timeout.body: Your code didn't finish within {seconds} seconds, so it was stopped. This time there's no line number to go on. Usually a loop never reaches its stopping condition and keeps going. Check that the value in your while condition changes every time the loop runs.
data.error.Timeout.detective: I see footprints going round and round the same spot. The code didn't finish within {seconds} seconds. The likely culprit: a loop that never reaches its stopping condition. Track whether the value in the condition really changes on every loop.
data.error.Timeout.title: Time's up
data.error.TypeError.body: You're mixing types that don't go together (from line {line}). This usually happens when you join a string and a number with +. Try matching the types: use int() to do math, or str() to join them as text.
data.error.TypeError.detective: Two values that don't belong together were caught side by side. The trail starts from line {line}. Mixing a string and a number as-is is the prime suspect. Check each value's ID (string or number?) and match the types with int() or str().
data.error.TypeError.title: Mismatched types ({type})
data.error.ValueError.body: The value is the right type, but Python can't use it (from line {line}). For example, int() got text that isn't a number, or a chart has a different number of names and values. Read the error message above first. If you were turning text into a number, check that it has no spaces between the digits and no decimal point (like 3.5).
data.error.ValueError.detective: A value that looks fine on the outside was hiding something. The case starts from line {line}. Did a string that can't become a number slip into int()? Or do the chart's names and values not match in count? Spaces between digits and decimal points (3.5) are suspects too. Call that value in with print() and question it.
data.error.ValueError.title: Unusable value ({type})
data.error._default.body: This is an error I haven't seen before. [[Let's start with the line number. ]]The trouble came from line {line}. The last line of the original message above tells you what went wrong.
data.error._default.detective: This is an error I haven't seen before. [[Let's start with the line number. ]]The case started from line {line}. The last line of the original message is the key testimony, and the best clue.
data.error._default.title: {type}
